draft.title: The 1920s and modern life
card: In the 1920s, new technology changed daily life in countries such as the United States, Britain and Australia. Cars, radio and cinema became part of ordinary life for many people.
Cars let people travel further and faster, so more people could live away from where they worked. Radio brought news, music and sport into the home at the same time for many listeners.
Cinema was cheap entertainment for large audiences. Jazz music and new dances spread through records, radio and dance halls.
Many young people took up these new styles and ideas. Older people often saw this as a challenge to traditional values and manners.
draft.remember: New technology and popular culture changed daily life, and young people often led the way.

a.q: Why did radio change daily life in the 1920s?
opts: It let many people hear the same news and music at home
It replaced the need for newspapers and cinemas
It let people travel further from their workplaces
It was owned by every family in every country
a.why: Radio brought the same news, music and sport into homes at the same time. It did not replace newspapers or cinema, and it was not in every home.
a.clue: Think about what radio brought into the home.

b.q: In 1926, Hana's grandparents in a small town are upset that she goes to a dance hall to hear jazz and wears new fashions. What does this best show?
opts: Young people challenging older ways through new culture
Older people leading the spread of new technology
Cars forcing families to move away from towns
Cinema replacing dance halls as the main entertainment
b.why: Hana is taking up new music and styles, and her grandparents see them as a break from tradition. The case is about generations and values, not about cars or cinema.
b.clue: Look at who likes the new styles and who objects.

a.best: It let many people hear the same news and music at home

b.best: Young people challenging older ways through new culture

problems.detail: The distractor 'Cars forcing families to move away from towns' uses 'forcing', while the card only says cars let people live further from work. It is a wrong option, but it brings in absolute wording the card does not use.
